concepts.name: Founding & rise
facts: Tradition says Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus.
Rome was a republic before it became an empire.
Augustus became the first Roman emperor in 27 BCE.

concepts.name: Daily life
facts: Roman cities had public baths where people met and relaxed.
Romans built long, straight roads across their empire.
Latin was the language of Rome.

concepts.name: Army & government
facts: A Roman legion had about 5,000 soldiers.
The Senate advised Rome's leaders and debated its laws.
Roman soldiers also built roads, bridges and forts.

concepts.name: Decline & legacy
facts: The western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.
The eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.
Many European languages grew out of Latin.

questions.prompt: According to legend, who founded the city of Rome?
questions.hint: He and his twin brother were raised by a wolf.
questions.explanation: Legend says Romulus founded Rome in 753 BCE after a quarrel with his twin brother Remus.

questions.prompt: Which river flows through the city of Rome?
questions.hint: It is a river in central Italy.
questions.explanation: Rome grew up on the banks of the Tiber river in central Italy.

questions.prompt: Who became the first Roman emperor?
questions.hint: He was Julius Caesar's adopted heir.
questions.explanation: Augustus became emperor in 27 BCE. Julius Caesar was a dictator but never an emperor.

questions.prompt: Which system ruled Rome from 509 BCE until Augustus?
questions.hint: Citizens elected officials called consuls.
questions.explanation: From 509 BCE Rome was a republic run by elected officials. Augustus ended it by becoming emperor.

questions.prompt: Which wars did Rome fight against Carthage?
questions.hint: Hannibal crossed the Alps in one of them.
questions.explanation: Rome fought Carthage in the three Punic Wars (264 to 146 BCE) and finally destroyed the city.

questions.prompt: What did Julius Caesar do in 49 BCE that began a civil war?
questions.hint: It was a small river on the border of Italy.
questions.explanation: Caesar led his army across the Rubicon river in 49 BCE. This broke Roman law and began a civil war.

questions.prompt: Roman tradition says Rome was founded in 753 BCE.
questions.hint: Think about the old legend of Rome's start.
questions.explanation: Romans dated the founding of their city to 753 BCE. The date comes from legend, not hard proof.

questions.prompt: Julius Caesar was the first Roman emperor.
questions.hint: Think about his adopted heir.
questions.explanation: Caesar was a dictator. His heir Augustus became the first emperor.

questions.prompt: Rome began as a small city in Italy.
questions.hint: Think about where great empires start.
questions.explanation: Rome started as a small settlement on the Tiber and slowly grew into a huge empire.

questions.prompt: How did the Roman Republic become an empire? Choose each next step.
questions.hint: Think about who ruled after Caesar was killed.
questions.explanation: Caesar became dictator, was murdered in 44 BCE, and his heir Octavian won the civil wars. In 27 BCE he took the name Augustus.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first.
questions.hint: All of these dates are BCE, so the biggest number comes first.
questions.explanation: Legend dates Rome to 753 BCE, the republic began in 509 BCE, Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and Augustus became emperor in 27 BCE.

questions.prompt: What was the Colosseum mainly used for?
questions.hint: Crowds came to watch.
questions.explanation: The Colosseum hosted gladiator fights and other shows for tens of thousands of people.

questions.prompt: Which language did the Romans speak?
questions.hint: French and Spanish grew out of it.
questions.explanation: Latin was the language of Rome. French, Spanish and Italian later grew out of it.

questions.prompt: What did Romans build to bring fresh water to towns?
questions.hint: Many were tall stone bridges with arches.
questions.explanation: Aqueducts carried water from hills into Roman towns, often over arched stone bridges.

questions.prompt: What were Roman public baths used for?
questions.hint: Think about relaxing and talking.
questions.explanation: Baths were social places where Romans washed, exercised and chatted with friends.

questions.prompt: What did the saying 'bread and circuses' describe?
questions.hint: Rulers wanted the poor to stay happy.
questions.explanation: Rulers gave the poor cheap grain and exciting shows to keep them content and calm.

questions.prompt: Roman concrete used volcanic ash. What could it do?
questions.hint: Think of harbours and piers.
questions.explanation: Concrete made with volcanic ash could harden underwater, so many Roman harbours and piers survive today.

questions.prompt: Roman gladiators fought in arenas such as the Colosseum.
questions.hint: Think about famous shows in Rome.
questions.explanation: Gladiators fought in arenas in front of crowds, and the Colosseum was the biggest one.

questions.prompt: Everyone in the Roman Empire had equal rights.
questions.hint: Think about slaves and free people.
questions.explanation: Rome had slaves, free citizens and non-citizens, and their rights were very different.

questions.prompt: Romans heated some buildings with hot air under the floor.
questions.hint: Think about warm baths in cold places.
questions.explanation: A system called the hypocaust sent hot air under floors and through walls to heat baths and rich homes.

questions.prompt: Roman numerals have a symbol for zero.
questions.hint: Look at I, V, X, L, C, D and M.
questions.explanation: Roman numerals have no zero. They use only the letters I, V, X, L, C, D and M.

questions.prompt: Write 14 in Roman numerals. Choose each step.
questions.hint: Split the number into tens and ones.
questions.explanation: 14 is 10 plus 4. X is 10 and IV is 4, so 14 is written XIV.

questions.prompt: Put these Roman numerals in order, smallest first.
questions.hint: Turn each numeral into a number first.
questions.explanation: IX is 9, XIV is 14, XL is 40 and C is 100.

questions.prompt: What was the main unit of the Roman army called?
questions.hint: About 5,000 soldiers made one.
questions.explanation: A legion had roughly 5,000 soldiers. A phalanx was a Greek battle formation.

questions.prompt: What was the Roman Senate?
questions.hint: Powerful men met to debate laws.
questions.explanation: The Senate was a council of senior Romans that debated laws and advised Rome's officials.

questions.prompt: How many consuls led the Roman Republic each year?
questions.hint: Power was shared so one man could not rule alone.
questions.explanation: Romans elected two consuls each year, so no single person held all the power.

questions.prompt: What did Roman soldiers also do besides fighting?
questions.hint: Think about what a legion left behind.
questions.explanation: Legions built roads, bridges, walls and forts, which also helped spread Roman rule.

questions.prompt: What did Hadrian's Wall defend?
questions.hint: It crosses northern England.
questions.explanation: Hadrian's Wall marked the northern frontier of Roman Britain. Building began around 122 CE.

questions.prompt: In the Roman army, what was 'decimation' as a punishment?
questions.hint: Think of the Latin word for ten.
questions.explanation: Decimation meant that one soldier in every ten, chosen by lot, was executed to punish a whole unit.

questions.prompt: A Roman legion had about 5,000 soldiers.
questions.hint: Think of a big group of soldiers.
questions.explanation: A legion was a large unit of roughly 5,000 soldiers.

questions.prompt: The Senate helped govern Rome.
questions.hint: Think about who debated Rome's laws.
questions.explanation: The Senate was a council of leading Romans that advised officials and shaped Rome's laws.

questions.prompt: Roman emperors were chosen by a public vote every year.
questions.hint: Think about who chose the consuls.
questions.explanation: Emperors ruled for life. Power passed by inheritance, adoption or force. Consuls were the ones elected each year.

questions.prompt: Julius Caesar was killed by Roman senators.
questions.hint: Think about the Ides of March.
questions.explanation: A group of senators stabbed Caesar in 44 BCE because they feared he wanted to be king.

questions.prompt: Rome has 3 legions of 5,000 soldiers. How many soldiers is that?
questions.hint: Equal groups means multiply.
questions.explanation: 3 legions of 5,000 soldiers is 3 x 5,000 = 15,000 soldiers.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first.
questions.hint: They run from 264 BCE to 212 CE.
questions.explanation: The Punic Wars began in 264 BCE, Caesar was murdered in 44 BCE, Hadrian's Wall was begun around 122 CE and Caracalla's edict came in 212 CE.

questions.prompt: In which year is the fall of the Western Roman Empire usually dated?
questions.hint: It was long after Rome's golden age.
questions.explanation: In 476 CE the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was removed by the leader Odoacer.

questions.prompt: Which city became the capital of the eastern Roman Empire?
questions.hint: Today it is called Istanbul.
questions.explanation: Emperor Constantine made Constantinople, now Istanbul, a new capital in 330 CE.

questions.prompt: Which group of languages grew out of Latin?
questions.hint: Spanish and French belong to it.
questions.explanation: French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian all grew out of Latin.

questions.prompt: Which group sacked Rome in 410 CE?
questions.hint: Their leader was called Alaric.
questions.explanation: In 410 CE the Visigoths under Alaric entered Rome and plundered the city.

questions.prompt: Which emperor made Christianity legal in the Roman Empire?
questions.hint: He ruled in the early 300s.
questions.explanation: Constantine and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, ending the persecution of Christians.

questions.prompt: The West fell in 476 CE. What happened to the Eastern Empire?
questions.hint: Its capital was Constantinople.
questions.explanation: The eastern empire, later called Byzantine, lasted nearly 1,000 years more, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

questions.prompt: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.
questions.hint: Think about the late 400s.
questions.explanation: The last western emperor was removed in 476 CE, the usual date for the fall of the West.

questions.prompt: Latin is still the everyday language of Italy today.
questions.hint: Think about what Italians speak now.
questions.explanation: Italians speak Italian. It grew out of Latin, but Latin itself is no longer an everyday language.

questions.prompt: The Eastern Roman Empire ended at the same time as the Western one.
questions.hint: Think about Constantinople.
questions.explanation: The eastern empire lasted until 1453, nearly 1,000 years after the West fell.

questions.prompt: Roman arches and domes still inspire modern buildings.
questions.hint: Think about government buildings today.
questions.explanation: Roman builders perfected the arch and the dome, and architects still use both ideas today.

questions.prompt: How many years passed between the fall of the West (476) and the East (1453)?
questions.hint: Take the earlier date from the later date.
questions.explanation: 1453 - 476 = 977, so the East lasted 977 years longer than the West.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first.
questions.hint: They run from 313 CE to 476 CE.
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan was in 313, Constantinople became a capital in 330, the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 and the West fell in 476.

questions.prompt: Step only on Roman emperors.
questions.hint: An emperor ruled after the Republic ended.
questions.explanation: Augustus, Nero, Trajan, Hadrian and Constantine were emperors. Caesar was a dictator, Cicero a speaker, Spartacus a gladiator, Hannibal a Carthaginian, Pompey a general.

questions.prompt: Step only on things the ancient Romans had.
questions.hint: Think of what existed about 2000 years ago.
questions.explanation: The Romans had public baths, aqueducts, concrete, Roman numerals and underfloor heating (the hypocaust). Potatoes came from the Americas and the rest were invented much later.

questions.prompt: Step only on Roman jobs and ranks.
questions.hint: Pharaohs, samurai and knights belong to other places.
questions.explanation: Centurions and legionaries served in the army; senators, consuls and tribunes held office in Rome. A pharaoh was Egyptian, a hoplite Greek, a samurai Japanese.

questions.prompt: Step only on events after the fall of Western Rome (476 CE).
questions.hint: Western Rome fell in 476 CE. Look at each date.
questions.explanation: Charlemagne (800), the Normans (1066), the First Crusade (1096), Magna Carta (1215) and the Black Death (1347) came later. The others were in the Roman period.
